clue.text: Bring order to main prison

blocks.note: to marshal is to arrange or bring into order
the main is a poetic word for the open sea

explanation.surface: Someone is told to restore discipline in the principal jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' reads as an adjective for the prison, but it is a noun for the ocean. The Marshalsea was a debtors' prison in Southwark, London, made famous by Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marshalsea was a notorious London jail, the one where Dickens's father was held for debt.

clue.text: Each bishop, for example, takes a book of services to church

blocks.note: taken as written
the pie was a pre-Reformation book of rules for church services
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Every bishop carries a service book to church.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle phrase adds a second hint: a chess bishop is a piece, and the answer is that word with A in front. The pie was the old book of rules for church services.
explanation.definitionFit: Apiece means for every one, as in 'a pound apiece', the same as each.

clue.text: Regal circle is assembled in the old palace

indicators.note: things assembled are put together from parts, so these letters are built into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
O is the shape of a circle
taken as written

explanation.surface: A royal court gathers in an ancient palace.
explanation.definitionFit: A seraglio was the women's quarters of an Ottoman palace, or the sultan's palace itself, in Constantinople.

clue.text: Quarrelled with spiteful woman in changed circumstances

indicators.note: one item said to be in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: circumstances that have changed have been altered
a cat is a spiteful woman, as in 'catty'

explanation.surface: Someone fell out with a malicious woman once things had changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circumstances' only fills out the surface; changed is the word that supplies the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To altercate is to dispute angrily or argue heatedly, an old verb for having a row.

clue.text: Second lid or bung for container

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
lid is slang for a hat, and a topper is a top hat

explanation.surface: A spare cap or plug for a jar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lid' seems to mean a cover for the container, but it is slang for a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopper is a plug fitted into the neck of a bottle or jar to seal it shut.

clue.text: Leader of Muslim's put in appearance here

definitions.text: Leader of Muslim's put in appearance here

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
something put in another thing is placed inside it

blocks.note: the first letter of Muslim
an air is a manner or appearance, as in an air of mystery

explanation.surface: A Muslim ruler makes an appearance at this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: the result is itself a leader of Muslims.
explanation.definitionFit: An amir, or emir, is a Muslim commander, governor or prince, a title used across the Islamic world.

clue.text: Display American volume at one assembly of scholars

blocks.note: liter is the American spelling of litre, a measure of volume
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A US book is put on show at a gathering of academics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' suggests a book, but here it is a unit of capacity.
explanation.definitionFit: The literati are learned, well-read people as a class, the intellectual elite of writers and critics.

clue.text: He provided innovative style, obviously

indicators.note: something innovative is new and different, so the word is remade in a fresh order

blocks.note: a he is a male, a man
provided that means if
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A designer clearly supplied a new look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Provided' looks like a verb meaning supplied, but it is the conjunction.
explanation.definitionFit: Manifestly means plainly or evidently, in a way anyone can see at once.

clue.text: Saw the first of Alpine peaks

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is wanted

blocks.note: a saw is an old saying, a proverb
the opening letter of Alpine

explanation.surface: A traveller glimpsed the leading summits of the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is a noun meaning a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Maxima are the highest values of a curve or quantity, the mathematical high points or tops.

clue.text: Animal's return after liberation revealed in book

indicators.note: a return is a going back, so the animal's name is read from its end

blocks.note: Lib is the short form of liberation, as in women's lib
the otter is the animal

explanation.surface: A freed animal comes back, and the story is told in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed animal follows the abbreviation, as 'after' says.
explanation.definitionFit: The libretto is the written text, or book, of an opera or musical, with words to be sung.

clue.text: Italian artist and architect inspire a transformation

indicators.note: a transformation changes the form of something, so the preceding letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged, the A included

explanation.surface: An Italian creator's work spurs a change in others.
explanation.walkthrough: The A does double duty in the surface as an article, but it belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Battista Piranesi was an eighteenth-century Italian etcher and architect famous for Roman views and imaginary prisons.

clue.text: Remove outer protection of fortified tower

blocks.note: first meaning: strip off a skin or rind
second meaning: a small square defensive tower of the Scottish borders

explanation.surface: Attackers strip the defences from a stronghold.
explanation.walkthrough: A peel tower is a fortified house built on the Anglo-Scottish border against raiders.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to strip off skin or rind; the noun names a small border keep built for defence.

clue.text: It's best on an isolated patch for this thief

blocks.note: the pick of a group is the best of it
a pocket is a small isolated area, as in a pocket of resistance

explanation.surface: A thief's ideal is a quiet spot to work alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patch' suggests a criminal's territory, but the isolated patch is the pocket the thief targets.
explanation.definitionFit: A pickpocket steals money and wallets from people's clothing, usually in crowds.

clue.text: Dish featured in magazine is a sort of tart

blocks.note: first meaning: glamour photographs of attractive women, a 'dish' being a good-looking person
second meaning: a sweet pastry dessert made with soft cheese

explanation.surface: A recipe in a food magazine turns out to be a kind of pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' and 'tart' both seem culinary, but the first is slang for an attractive person, pictured in magazine pin-ups.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for pin-up photography of attractive women, and also names a baked dessert on a biscuit base.

clue.text: Dickensian seducer put to sea at the helm

blocks.note: the person at the helm steers the ship
a ship putting to sea goes forth from harbour

explanation.surface: A rogue from Dickens takes a boat out and steers it.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay pieces come in reverse order. Steerforth is the charming villain of David Copperfield who seduces Little Em'ly.
explanation.definitionFit: James Steerforth in David Copperfield elopes with and abandons Little Em'ly, making him the novel's seducer.

clue.text: Accountant sounds warning for US partnership

blocks.note: CA stands for chartered accountant
a car horn hoots to warn others

explanation.surface: A bookkeeper raises the alarm about an American business partnership.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is used in the phrase 'in cahoots', originally American, for a secret alliance.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in cahoots means being in league or collusion with someone, an American colloquial word for partnership.

clue.text: Don is showing his agitation

definitions.note: a noun for a person; the answer here is used as a noun

blocks.note: taken as written
panic is a state of agitation

explanation.surface: An Oxford tutor visibly loses his composure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a university lecturer or a verb for putting on, but it is the Spanish title for a gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Don is the Spanish honorific for a man, so a Don is a Spanish speaker, a Hispanic.

clue.text: To carry on some papers is tough

indicators.note: only part of the following words is taken, a run of letters within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of papers, all of is, and the start of tough

explanation.surface: Keeping going with a pile of paperwork is hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To persist is to continue or keep going steadily despite difficulty, the same as to keep at something.

clue.text: Dramatist is heard to be involved with new production

indicators.note: what is heard is spoken, so the meaning of the following words counts by its sound

blocks.note: to have shared in a new production is to have been involved with it

explanation.surface: A playwright is rumoured to be working on a new staging.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote The Rivals and The School for Scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan was an Irish-born eighteenth-century playwright, author of comedies such as The School for Scandal.

clue.text: It can be mean to proclaim a lady's secret

definitions.note: a definition by description; the answer is a noun or adjective

blocks.note: to aver is to declare or assert
by old convention a lady never tells her age

explanation.surface: It can be unkind to announce how old a woman is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like unkind, but it is the arithmetic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An average is the arithmetic mean of a set of numbers, found by dividing the total by the count.

clue.text: Old fashioned port is disregarded

blocks.note: passé is French for out of date
Dover is the English Channel port

explanation.surface: A dated harbour town is ignored by travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' tempts as the fortified wine, but it is the Kent ferry port.
explanation.definitionFit: To be passed over is to be ignored or overlooked, for instance when a promotion goes to someone else.

clue.text: Like a piece of cake - alternatively, last of pie, say?

indicators.note: only the final letter of the next word is wanted
alternatively suggests another way of putting things, so the word is reordered

blocks.note: the closing letter of pie
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Something is as simple as cake, or perhaps the last bit of pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like the usual signal for an example, but here it is the word to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: 'A piece of cake' is an idiom for a task needing no effort, so like one means simple.

clue.text: Record-holder - some jumper!

blocks.note: first meaning: the cardboard cover a vinyl record is kept in
second meaning: part of a sweater, the piece covering the arm

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a champion high jumper; a jumper is the British word for a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeve is both the paper or card cover of a gramophone disc and the arm portion of a garment.

clue.text: Crime writer who deals in what's wicked?

blocks.note: first meaning: Raymond, the American author of hard-boiled detective novels
second meaning: a trader in candles, things that have wicks, read as wick-ed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' looks like evil, fitting crime, but is read as 'having wicks'; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Raymond Chandler created Philip Marlowe; a chandler is a dealer in candles, which are fitted with wicks.

clue.text: Pool's smelly if nothing sinks to the bottom

indicators.note: in a down entry, something sinking to the bottom moves from the top to the end

blocks.note: olid is a rare word for foul-smelling
nothing is the letter O, here the one already at the front that moves

explanation.surface: A swimming pool stinks if no one cleans the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Moving the O from the front of OLID to the end gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lido is a public open-air swimming pool, named after the Venice beach resort.

clue.text: A poet's contracts

blocks.note: taken as written
Robert Bridges was Poet Laureate; the possessive adds no letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracts' looks like a noun for agreements, but it is a verb, matching a poet's name with the possessive ending absorbed in the S.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a text is to shorten or condense it, so it is a verb for reducing in length.

clue.text: Sent abroad English team under guidance

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a cricket or football team has eleven players, XI in Roman numerals
being led is being under someone's guidance

explanation.surface: An English side tours overseas with a manager in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone exiled is banished from their homeland and forced to live in another country.

clue.text: Unstinting author writing in dictionary

indicators.note: one thing placed in another means the first sits inside the second

blocks.note: the pen is what authors write with, standing for the writer
a person's hand is their handwriting
OED is the Oxford English Dictionary

explanation.surface: A writer generously contributes to a dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Pen stands for an author by metonymy, as in 'a hired pen'; hand for handwriting. Both go together inside the Oxford English Dictionary's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-handed person gives freely and generously, holding nothing back, just as an unstinting giver does.
